name: Mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati)
method_summary: Vism VIII, opening of the section: the Buddha's praise (peaceful and sublime, unadulterated, a pleasant abiding, making arisen evil unwholesome states disappear at once) and the formula of sixteen bases in four tetrads; a beginner uses the first tetrad, the other three are for one who has attained jhāna. The meditator goes to a forest, a tree root or an empty place (the forest suits it since the breath is the post to which the mind is tied by the rope of mindfulness, and village noise is a thorn to jhāna), sits cross-legged with the body upright and mindfulness established in front, and breathes in and out mindfully, knowing long and short breaths by duration, experiencing the whole breath-body and calming the bodily formation. The text sets a five-link learning (learning, questioning, establishing, absorption, characteristic) and an attention in stages: counting, connecting, touching, fixing, noting, turning away, purification and looking back; counting and connecting are described in the two practices below.
prerequisites: Virtue purified, minor impediments cut, the subject learnt from a teacher in five links, a fit lodging, the meal done and its drowsiness dispelled, the mind gladdened by recollecting the Triple Gem (Vism VIII p. 277-278).
notes: Contribution from the selected pages 266-281 (the word commentary on the first tetrad's first steps, pp. 272-277, is included). No breath-holding is described on these pages.

name: Counting the breath (gaṇanā), first attention of mindfulness of breathing
method_summary: First of the stages of attention (Vism VIII p. 278-280). The beginner counts the breaths as they are noticed: first slowly, like a grain-measurer, then, when the breaths are evident, quickly, like a herdsman counting cattle at the gate, taking only the breaths at the place they touch (the gate), not following them inside or outside; for a subject bound by counting, consciousness becomes one-pointed by the power of counting, like a boat held in a strong current by a rudder. The counting continues until, even without counting, mindfulness stays on the in- and out-breath; its purpose is only to cut off scattered outside thoughts and establish mindfulness on the object.

warnings.text:
pañcannaṃ heṭṭhā na ṭhapetabbaṃ, dasannaṃ  
upari na netabbaṃ, antarā khaṇḍaṃ na dassetabbaṃ|

notes: The text's own reasons: below five consciousness struggles in a cramped space; above ten it depends on the counting; a gap makes the mind waver whether the subject has reached its peak.

name: Connecting (anubandhanā), following the breath, in mindfulness of breathing
method_summary: Second stage of attention (Vism VIII p. 280-281): counting withdrawn, one follows the in- and out-breaths continuously with mindfulness, not by following their beginning, middle and end (for the out-breath navel, heart, nose-tip; for the in-breath the reverse) but by touching and fixing: attending to the place touched. The text gives three similes: the lame man seated at the foot of a swing who sees both ends and the middle of the plank without going after them; the doorkeeper who examines only those who reach the gate; and the saw (a man sawing a log fixes mindfulness on the saw-teeth where they touch the log).

warnings.text:
tañ ca kho na ādimajjhapariyo-  
sānānugamanavasena|

assāsādimajjhapariyosānaṃ satiyā anugacchato ajjhat-  
taṃ vikkhepagatena cittena kāyo pi cittam pi sāraddhā ca honti  
iñjitā ca phanditā ca|

notes: The warning quoted is the text's own (from the Paṭisambhidāmagga): following the breath's beginning, middle and end scatters the mind and agitates body and mind.

name: Loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā)
method_summary: Vism IX, from the opening to the breaking down of the barriers: the beginner, having cut impediments and taken the subject, sits at ease after the meal in a secluded place and first reflects on the danger in hate and the benefit of patience. Loving-kindness is developed first toward oneself ('may I be happy and free from suffering'), as one's own witness; then toward a dear and respected person; then, to break down the barriers, toward a very dear friend, a neutral person and an enemy, making the mind soft and workable at each step. It is not developed first toward a disliked person, a very dear friend, a neutral person or an enemy, not specifically toward one of the opposite sex, and not at all toward the dead. If resentment arises, the text gives an ordered set of remedies (prc:patigha-vinodana-vism). The barrier is broken when the mind is even toward oneself and the three others (the bandits test); then the sign and access arise, and absorption follows (the first jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness, and the higher ones), after which the directions are pervaded (Vism IX p. 307-308).

warnings.text:
ayaṃ hi mettā appiya-  
puggale atippiyasahāyake majjhatte verīpuggale ti imesu  
catūsu paṭhamaṃ na bhāvetabbā; lingavisabhāge odhiso  
na bhāvetabbā, kālankate na bhāvetabbā va|

notes: Contribution from the selected pages; the eleven benefits quoted by the text and the near and far enemies are in other entries.
signs_of_progress: The text's mark that the barrier is broken: the mind is equal toward oneself, the dear, the neutral and the enemy, so that if bandits demanded one of the four no one is chosen (Vism IX p. 307); at that moment the sign and access are gained.

name: Removing resentment in the development of loving-kindness (Vism IX)
method_summary: Vism IX gives an ordered set of remedies for resentment (āghāta, paṭigha) that arises on turning loving-kindness to an enemy, each to be used if the one before does not calm the mind: return repeatedly to loving-kindness for the earlier persons; recall the Buddha's advice (the saw simile, the verse on not returning anger, the seven things that please an enemy); recall a calm quality in the person (bodily, verbal or mental conduct), or set up compassion if none is calm; admonish oneself in verse; reflect on ownership of kamma (his and one's own); recall the Teacher's earlier patience in the Jātakas; reflect that in the beginningless round the person has been mother, father, relative; reflect on the eleven benefits of loving-kindness; analyse the person into elements, aggregates and bases; and share gifts. The text refers to the Āghātapaṭivinaya-sutta for five other ways.
notes: New sense-specific entry for the Visuddhimagga's list; the stories of the Bodhisatta's patience are told in the text as examples, not as bodily practices.

name: Good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā), the teacher who gives the subject
method_summary: Vism III: the meditation subject is taken from a good friend (kalyāṇamitta), described by a verse as dear, respected, one who can be developed, a speaker, patient with speech, able to speak on the profound and not urging to what is unfit; the Buddha is the best, then an arahant of the eighty great disciples, then a non-returner down to a one-Piṭaka holder who is conscientious (lajjī) and holds the teachers' tradition. Approach with the proper duties, ask at the proper time, state one's own temperament truthfully, and surrender oneself to the Buddha or the teacher; the teacher, knowing or asking the pupil's temperament, teaches the subject that suits it.
notes: Contribution from Vism III. The order of preference of teachers is the commentator's.

name: The earth kasiṇa (pathavī-kasiṇa), taking the learning sign (Vism IV p. 125)
method_summary: Vism IV p. 125: the meditator looks at the prepared disk with the eyes opened evenly (as when looking at one's face in a mirror), not too wide and not too little; does not reflect on the colour or the mark but sets the mind on the concept 'earth' (pathavī), repeating it, opening and closing the eyes by turns until the learning sign arises (seen with the eyes shut as clearly as with them open). After that he develops it in his own dwelling; if the young concentration is lost he returns to the place, takes the sign again and continues. As he does so the hindrances are suppressed, the defilements subside, the mind is concentrated by access concentration and the counterpart sign arises.

warnings.text:
ati-ummīlayato hi cakkhu kilamati, maṇḍalañ ca ativi-  
bhūtaṃ hoti, ten'; assa nimittaṃ nuppajjati| atimandaṃ  
ummīlayato maṇḍalaṃ avibhūtaṃ hoti, cittañ ca līnaṃ  
hoti, evam pi nimittaṃ nuppajjati

notes: The text's continuation on the difference between the two signs is on p. 126, not included.
signs_of_progress: The learning sign (uggahanimitta) arises when the disk with eyes closed comes into focus as when open; then, with the hindrances suppressed and access reached, the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta).

name: Contemplation of the foul (asubha-bhāvanā): summary only
method_summary: Summary only (restricted). In Vism III the ten foulnesses are ten kinds of corpse (bloated, livid, festering, cut up, gnawed, scattered, hacked and scattered, bleeding, worm-infested, skeleton). Vism III names them among the forty subjects, as bringing absorption (first jhāna only), as suitable for the greedy temperament, as taken by sight, and as not to be enlarged. No method is given here.

warnings.text: ḍhitesu kuṇaparāsi yeva vaḍḍhati, na koci ānisaṃso atthi|

notes: Restricted practice: only the text's own cautions on not enlarging the sign are recorded; no procedure, and it is not recommended.

name: Mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati): summary only
method_summary: Summary only (restricted). Vism III lists mindfulness occupied with the body among the ten recollections and the forty subjects: it brings the first jhāna (with the foulnesses), suits the greedy temperament, is taken partly by sight and partly by hearing, and is not to be enlarged. Vism VIII p. 266 closes its exposition with benefits stated by the text (mastery of discontent and fear, endurance of cold and heat, the four jhānas by the colours of the hair and the rest, the direct-knowledges). No method is given here.
notes: Restricted practice (works on the body's parts as repulsive); recorded by name and the text's cautions only.

name: Development of the four divine abidings (brahmavihāra)
method_summary: Vism IX p. 318-319: the four divine abidings are loving-kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity; the text gives each a mark, function, manifestation, proximate cause, success and failure, a common purpose (pleasant abiding in insight and success in existence) and a special purpose (loving-kindness against ill will, compassion against cruelty, gladness against discontent, equanimity against lust), and a near and a far enemy for each: for loving-kindness lust is near and ill will far; for compassion household-based displeasure near and cruelty far; for gladness household-based gladness near and discontent far; for equanimity the household-based equanimity of ignorance near, lust and resentment far. In Vism III they are listed among the forty, three (fourfold count) or the fourth jhāna, and suit the hating temperament.

warnings.text:
so lahum  
otāraṃ labhati, tasmā tato suṭṭhu mettā rakkhitabbā|

notes: Contribution; the practice itself (pervading the directions) is in prc:metta-bhavana and the Vism IX text beyond the selected pages.
